cues.text: Welcome to Chemical Thermodynamics.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Begin every energy calculation by choosing the system.
An open system exchanges matter and energy with its surroundings.
A closed system exchanges energy but not matter.
An isolated system exchanges neither.
Internal energy, enthalpy and entropy are state functions: their changes
depend
on initial and final states.
Heat and work describe energy transfer along a path.
Temperature and pressure are intensive properties; total volume and total
internal energy are extensive.
In the Chemistry convention, the first law is change in internal energy equals
heat plus work done on the system.
Heat entering is positive.
Compression work is positive, while expansion work is negative.
For expansion against a constant external pressure, work is minus external
pressure times the volume increase.
Consider a closed system that absorbs five hundred joules and expands by one
litre against two bar.
One litre bar equals one hundred joules.
The work is therefore minus two hundred joules, and the internal energy
increases by three hundred joules.
The system gained heat but returned some energy to the surroundings as work.
Notice that external pressure appears in this work expression.
If it varies, the appropriate pressure volume integral is needed.
Free expansion against zero external pressure does no pressure volume work.
Adiabatic means no heat transfer; it does not automatically mean constant
temperature.
Isothermal means constant temperature.
Isochoric means constant volume, and isobaric means constant pressure.
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature, so an
isothermal
change has zero internal energy change even though heat and work may each be
nonzero.
Keep the signs tied to the chosen system, and always convert litre bar into
energy units before adding heat and work.
Enthalpy is defined as internal energy plus pressure times volume.
For a closed system undergoing only pressure volume work at constant pressure,
the heat transferred equals the enthalpy change.
At constant volume, with no other work, heat equals the internal energy
change.
The conditions are part of the result.
An exothermic process has a negative enthalpy change, while an endothermic
process has a positive one.
For ideal gaseous reactants and products at the same temperature, the gas
contribution gives change in enthalpy equals change in internal energy plus
change in gaseous mole number times R T.
In ordinary reaction calculations this form neglects condensed phase pressure
volume contributions.
Count only gaseous species when finding the gaseous mole change.
For one nitrogen plus three hydrogen forming two ammonia, all gases, the
change
is two minus four, or minus two moles per reaction as written.
Suppose the internal energy change is minus ninety point zero kilojoules for
that reaction amount at three hundred kelvin.
Use R equal to zero point zero zero eight three one four kilojoules per mole
kelvin.
The correction is minus two times R times three hundred, about minus four
point
nine nine kilojoules.
The enthalpy change is about minus ninety five point zero kilojoules.
Reversing the reaction reverses both energy changes and the gaseous mole
change.
A separate useful relation for one mole of an ideal gas is molar heat capacity
at constant pressure minus molar heat capacity at constant volume equals R.
It is not a universal identity for liquids, solids or real gases.
Heat capacity relates heat to temperature change under specified conditions;
if
it varies appreciably with temperature, use an integral instead of a constant
value.
Check the phase labels and the reaction amount before substituting numbers.
Hess's law follows from enthalpy being a state function.
A reaction may be assembled from several steps; adding their enthalpy changes
gives the same overall change.
Reverse a step and reverse its sign.
Multiply an equation by a number and multiply its enthalpy by that number.
Here is an illustrative cycle.
Carbon as graphite plus oxygen forming carbon dioxide has enthalpy minus three
hundred ninety four kilojoules per mole of reaction.
Carbon monoxide plus half an oxygen forming carbon dioxide has enthalpy minus
two hundred eighty three.
We want graphite plus half an oxygen forming carbon monoxide.
Keep the first equation and reverse the second.
Carbon dioxide cancels, leaving the target reaction.
Add minus three hundred ninety four to plus two hundred eighty three to obtain
minus one hundred eleven kilojoules.
These rounded values illustrate the calculation; phases and reference
conditions must match.
Standard formation enthalpy refers to forming one mole of a substance from its
elements in their reference states.
The standard formation enthalpy of an element in its reference state is
assigned zero; this does not say that its internal energy or entropy is zero.
Multiply each formation enthalpy by its stoichiometric coefficient, then
subtract the reactant sum from the product sum.
Combustion enthalpy concerns complete burning of the specified amount, usually
one mole, with product phases stated.
Atomization creates gaseous atoms.
Sublimation converts solid to gas.
Ionization removes an electron from a gaseous species, while hydration brings
gaseous ions into water.
Dissolution can combine lattice separation and solvation effects.
For a gas phase bond estimate, add energies of bonds broken and subtract
energies of bonds formed.
Average bond enthalpies give an approximation because bond environments
differ.
Do not mix an average gas bond estimate with a liquid phase reaction without
accounting for phase changes.
Energy conservation alone does not choose the direction of a process.
Entropy supplies the second law criterion: a spontaneous change increases the
total entropy of the system and surroundings.
The system's entropy may decrease if the surroundings gain more.
A reversible ideal limit has zero total entropy production.
For a reversible isothermal path, entropy change is reversible heat divided by
temperature.
More generally, integrate reversible heat divided by temperature along a
suitable path between the states.
Entropy is a state function, even when the actual path is irreversible.
For the usual closed system at constant temperature and pressure, without
imposed non pressure volume work, a negative Gibbs energy change identifies a
thermodynamically favourable direction.
Gibbs energy change is enthalpy change minus temperature times entropy change.
Temperature must be in kelvin.
Match the energy units before subtracting.
Suppose enthalpy change is minus forty kilojoules and entropy change is minus
one hundred joules per kelvin.
Convert the entropy to minus zero point one zero zero kilojoules per kelvin.
At three hundred kelvin, Gibbs energy change is minus forty plus thirty, or
minus ten kilojoules.
At five hundred kelvin, it is minus forty plus fifty, or plus ten.
If both enthalpy and entropy changes are approximately temperature independent
over the range, the crossover is four hundred kelvin.
This exothermic process with decreasing entropy is favoured at lower
temperature.
Positive enthalpy and positive entropy favour higher temperature.
Negative enthalpy and positive entropy favour the forward direction throughout
the temperature range where those signs hold.
The opposite pair does not.
Finally, favourable does not mean fast.
A large activation barrier can make a thermodynamically favourable reaction
very slow.
Keep the direction question separate from the kinetics question.
The standard Gibbs energy change and the Gibbs energy change for the current
mixture are different quantities.
The connection is Gibbs energy change equals standard Gibbs energy change plus
R T times the natural logarithm of the reaction quotient Q.
The rigorous quotient uses dimensionless activities relative to standard
states.
For ideal dilute solutions and ideal gases, concentration or pressure ratios
provide useful approximations.
At equilibrium, the reaction Gibbs energy change is zero and Q equals the
equilibrium constant K.
Substitution gives standard Gibbs energy change equals minus R T times the
natural logarithm of K.
Thus a negative standard Gibbs energy change implies K greater than one at
that
temperature.
It does not guarantee that every possible mixture will proceed forward.
Take standard Gibbs energy change approximately minus five point seven four
four kilojoules per mole at three hundred kelvin.
With R equal to zero point zero zero eight three one four kilojoules per mole
kelvin, the natural logarithm of K is about two point three zero three.
K is approximately ten.
If Q is one, the forward direction is favoured.
If Q is one hundred, Gibbs energy change is positive, about plus five point
seven four kilojoules per mole, and the reverse direction is favoured.
If Q is ten, the mixture is at equilibrium.
Combining the equations gives Gibbs energy change equals R T times the natural
logarithm of Q divided by K.
This directly connects composition to direction.
Standard conditions do not automatically mean two hundred ninety eight kelvin;
always read the stated temperature.
Finish with a short checklist: define the system, choose the correct work
sign,
preserve reaction coefficients and phases, convert entropy units, and
distinguish Q from K.
Use the worked notes and six original practice questions.
This is the core Unit four foundation; detailed enthalpy cycles, entropy
integrals and wider mixed problems remain for further study.
Formation enthalpies let us assemble a reaction without measuring it directly.
Use the balanced coefficients and the physical states in the data.
For methane combustion to carbon dioxide gas and liquid water, take
illustrative standard formation enthalpies in kilojoules per mole: methane
minus seventy five, carbon dioxide minus three hundred ninety four, and liquid
water minus two hundred eighty six.
Oxygen in its reference state contributes zero.
Products contribute minus three hundred ninety four plus twice minus two
hundred eighty six, giving minus nine hundred sixty six.
Subtract the reactant contribution of minus seventy five.
The reaction enthalpy is minus eight hundred ninety one kilojoules per mole of
methane for these rounded data.
Changing the product to water vapour changes the answer.
Average bond enthalpies instead estimate energy for gas phase bonds broken
minus bonds formed.
They are approximate and do not automatically include condensation or solid
lattice effects.
An element's zero standard formation enthalpy applies to its reference state,
not to every allotrope, gaseous atom or ion.
Always label the amount and phase beside a thermochemical result.
An ionic dissolution cycle separates processes that are easily confused.
First imagine pulling the solid into separated gaseous ions.
Define this lattice dissociation enthalpy as positive.
Then hydrate those gaseous ions to the chosen aqueous reference states;
hydration enthalpies are normally negative.
Adding both stages gives the enthalpy of solution for matching endpoints and
concentration conventions.
With illustrative values of plus seven hundred eighty kilojoules per mole for
lattice dissociation and minus seven hundred fifty for total hydration,
dissolution has enthalpy plus thirty kilojoules per mole.
A positive result does not by itself prove that dissolution is impossible,
because the Gibbs energy also contains an entropy contribution.
Some tables instead define lattice enthalpy for forming the solid from gaseous
ions.
That is the opposite process and has the opposite sign.
Never insert a number until its process is clear.
Atomization, ionization and electron attachment provide further steps in a
full
Born Haber cycle.
Keep each species and charge balanced when adding them.
This two stage example isolates dissolution bookkeeping rather than claiming
to
reproduce every step of a complete formation cycle.
A calorimeter records a temperature change in material surrounding the
reacting
system.
Include every heat capacity specified in the problem.
Suppose one hundred grams of solution has specific heat capacity four point
two
joules per gram kelvin, and the calorimeter contributes eighty joules per
kelvin.
The combined heat capacity is four hundred twenty plus eighty, or five hundred
joules per kelvin.
A temperature rise of two kelvin means the measured surroundings gain one
thousand joules.
If heat loss is negligible, the reaction releases one thousand joules.
For zero point zero five zero mole reacting as written, the molar heat is
minus
twenty kilojoules per mole.
The negative sign belongs to the reaction, while the solution and vessel
gained
heat.
At approximately constant pressure with only pressure volume work, the
reaction
heat corresponds to enthalpy change.
In a rigid bomb calorimeter, the corresponding constant volume heat gives
internal energy change; convert to enthalpy when the gas mole correction is
required.
Check whether a supplied calorimeter constant already includes the solution
before adding its heat capacity again.
Entropy change must be evaluated using a reversible reference path between the
same endpoints.
Heat divided by temperature is not a universal expression for an arbitrary
irreversible transfer.
At an equilibrium phase transition at constant temperature and pressure, the
molar entropy change is the molar transition enthalpy divided by that
temperature.
For melting with illustrative enthalpy six kilojoules per mole at three
hundred
kelvin, the entropy increase is twenty joules per mole kelvin.
Freezing between the reverse endpoints gives minus twenty.
For warming a substance at constant pressure with approximately constant molar
heat capacity, integrate heat capacity divided by temperature.
The result is molar heat capacity times the natural logarithm of final
temperature divided by initial temperature.
With thirty joules per mole kelvin and warming from three hundred to six
hundred kelvin, the increase is thirty times the natural logarithm of two,
about twenty point eight joules per mole kelvin.
Both temperatures must be absolute.
If heat capacity varies appreciably, retain it inside the integral rather than
reusing the constant value shortcut.
A system can lose entropy while a spontaneous process increases the total
entropy of system and surroundings.
Consider an illustrative process at three hundred kelvin and constant pressure
that releases six kilojoules per mole into a large thermal reservoir.
Assume only pressure volume work and negligible changes elsewhere.
The reservoir receives six thousand joules per mole, so its entropy increases
by twenty joules per mole kelvin.
If the system entropy decreases by ten joules per mole kelvin, the total
increases by ten.
The process is thermodynamically favourable under those stated conditions.
Its Gibbs energy change is minus six kilojoules minus three hundred times
minus
zero point zero one zero kilojoules per kelvin, giving minus three kilojoules
per mole.
Negative temperature times the universe entropy change gives the same result
under these constraints.
The reservoir temperature is effectively constant; do not divide a large
varying temperature heat transfer by one arbitrary temperature.
This example also shows why exothermic and spontaneous are different labels.
Identify the surroundings, constraints and entropy contribution before using
the sign of heat as a direction test.
Work depends on the path even when an ideal gas begins and ends at the same
temperature and volumes.
Consider one mole at three hundred kelvin expanding from two to four litres.
For a reversible isothermal path, work done on the gas in the Chemistry sign
convention is minus n R T times the natural logarithm of two.
Using R eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin gives about minus
one
point seven two nine kilojoules.
Now compare an isothermal expansion against constant external pressure equal
to
the final ideal gas pressure.
The final pressure is n R T divided by the final volume.
Multiplying that pressure by the two litre volume increase gives work about
minus one point two four seven kilojoules.
Use compatible volume units in both factors.
The reversible path supplies a greater magnitude of expansion work between
these endpoints.
For the ideal gas, internal energy change is zero in both isothermal cases, so
heat entering balances the negative work.
Reversible does not mean zero work, and isothermal does not mean zero heat.
The comparison assumes only pressure volume work, the stated ideal gas model
and suitable heat exchange to maintain temperature.
Adiabatic means no heat transfer, not unchanged temperature.
As a supporting ideal gas application, take one mole of a monatomic gas
initially at three hundred kelvin.
Compress it reversibly and adiabatically to half its initial volume, using
constant molar heat capacities and gamma equal to five thirds.
The reversible ideal gas relation gives final temperature equal to three
hundred times two raised to the two thirds power, or about four hundred
seventy
six point two kelvin.
Internal energy rises by n C V times the temperature increase.
With C V equal to three halves R, the rise is about two point one nine eight
kilojoules using R eight point three one four.
Heat is zero, so work done on the gas is positive by that amount in the
Chemistry convention.
An irreversible adiabatic change still has zero heat, but it cannot
automatically use the same reversible volume temperature relation.
Likewise a gas with temperature dependent heat capacities needs a more careful
calculation.
State reversibility, ideal behaviour and constant heat capacities before
applying this power law.
The example reinforces first law signs rather than replacing the separate
Physics treatment of complete gas cycles.
A reaction enthalpy quoted at one temperature need not have exactly the same
value at another.
A Hess cycle can connect the temperatures by warming reactants and products
through their respective heat capacities.
The reaction heat capacity change is the sum of product heat capacities with
stoichiometric coefficients minus the corresponding reactant sum.
If that difference is approximately constant over the range and no phase
transition intervenes, the enthalpy correction is reaction heat capacity
change
times the temperature increase.
Take a supplied reaction enthalpy minus one hundred kilojoules per mole at two
hundred ninety eight kelvin and reaction heat capacity change plus fifty
joules
per mole kelvin.
Raising the temperature to three hundred ninety eight kelvin adds plus five
kilojoules per mole, so the corrected reaction enthalpy is minus ninety five.
The reaction remains exothermic in this model but is less exothermic at the
higher temperature.
Convert joules into kilojoules before adding.
If heat capacity varies, keep it inside the temperature integral; if a phase
transition occurs, include its enthalpy separately.
This is a supporting temperature correction derived from state functions, not
permission to extrapolate a constant heat capacity indefinitely.
Standard molar entropy values are combined with the balanced reaction
coefficients, not simply compared one species at a time.
Use the written reaction one nitrogen molecule plus three hydrogen molecules
giving two ammonia molecules, all gaseous.
Suppose supplied standard molar entropies are one hundred ninety two, one
hundred thirty one and one hundred ninety three joules per mole kelvin
for
nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia respectively.
The product sum is two times one hundred ninety three, or three hundred eighty
six.
The reactant sum is one hundred ninety two plus three times one hundred thirty
one, or five hundred eighty five.
Reaction entropy is therefore minus one hundred ninety nine joules per mole of
reaction kelvin.
All individual entropy values are positive while their reaction difference is
negative.
If the supplied reaction enthalpy is minus ninety two kilojoules per mole of
reaction at two hundred ninety eight kelvin, standard Gibbs energy is about
minus thirty two point seven kilojoules after converting the entropy units.
The coefficients define the reaction amount throughout.
This calculation uses the stated standard states and supplied rounded data,
not
a claim that every entropy can be inferred solely from counting gas molecules.
A constant volume heat measurement and a reaction enthalpy are not
automatically the same number.
For a closed reaction system with only pressure volume work, constant volume
heat gives internal energy change.
At constant pressure the corresponding heat gives enthalpy change under the
usual conditions.
Consider the supplied illustrative reaction data for two hydrogen molecules
plus one oxygen molecule forming two liquid water molecules at three hundred
kelvin.
Let internal energy change be minus five hundred sixty kilojoules per mole of
that written reaction.
Only gaseous species enter the ideal gas mole correction: there are zero
gaseous product moles and three gaseous reactant moles, so the change is minus
three.
Using R zero point zero zero eight three one four kilojoules per mole kelvin,
the enthalpy is minus five hundred sixty minus seven point four eight three,
or
about minus five hundred sixty seven point four eight kilojoules per mole of
reaction.
Producing one mole of liquid water corresponds to half the written reaction,
so
both energy changes must be halved for that basis.
Including liquid water in the gas count would give the wrong correction.
Preserve phases, coefficients and the stated reaction basis before comparing
heat measurements.
A reaction enthalpy belongs to a particular balanced equation.
Consider the supplied equation two moles of hydrogen plus one mole of oxygen
forming two moles of liquid water, with reaction enthalpy minus five hundred
seventy two kilojoules per mole of reaction extent.
Start with zero point three zero zero mole hydrogen and zero point one zero
zero mole oxygen.
Dividing each amount by its stoichiometric coefficient gives possible extents
zero point one five zero and zero point one zero zero mole.
Oxygen limits the extent to zero point one zero zero mole.
The reaction forms zero point two zero zero mole water and leaves zero point
one zero zero mole hydrogen.
At constant pressure with only pressure volume work, the reaction heat is
minus
fifty seven point two kilojoules.
Writing the equation for one mole water halves its reaction enthalpy but
doubles the numerical extent for the same physical conversion.
Their product stays unchanged.
Distinguish reaction extent from product amount, and keep the written
coefficient convention attached to every molar reaction enthalpy.
At a phase transition carried out reversibly at its equilibrium temperature
and
pressure, the entropy change is the transition enthalpy divided by the
absolute
transition temperature.
Use supplied illustrative fusion enthalpy six point zero zero kilojoules per
mole at three hundred kelvin.
Melting two point zero zero moles absorbs twelve point zero kilojoules and
raises the system entropy by forty point zero joules per kelvin.
A thermal reservoir at the same temperature loses forty point zero joules per
kelvin in the reversible limit.
The total is zero, consistent with equilibrium rather than a finite
thermodynamic driving force.
Freezing reverses both signs for the same endpoints.
This shortcut uses the transition temperature, not an arbitrary room
temperature.
Away from phase equilibrium, use an appropriate reversible reference path with
heating or cooling stages as needed.
A positive entropy change of the sample alone does not establish spontaneity,
because the surroundings must also be included.
State the phase, amount, pressure and transition temperature before applying
the ratio.
Heat transferred across a finite temperature difference produces entropy even
when energy is conserved.
Suppose an isolated combined model contains ideal reservoirs at four hundred
and three hundred kelvin.
One thousand joules flows from the hot reservoir to the cold reservoir, with
no
work and no energy loss elsewhere.
The hot reservoir loses two point five zero joules per kelvin of entropy.
The cold reservoir gains three point three three joules per kelvin.
Their total entropy change is positive zero point eight three three joule per
kelvin.
The two energy changes cancel, but the entropy changes do not, because equal
heat is divided by different temperatures.
Reversing only this heat transfer would make the combined entropy change
negative and cannot happen spontaneously in the isolated model.
A refrigerator can move heat in that direction only with additional processes
and an energy supply.
The reservoir approximation means each temperature stays essentially constant
during the transfer.
Finite bodies that noticeably change temperature require integration rather
than using these two fixed denominators.
Standard reaction Gibbs energy describes standard states, while actual
direction also depends on composition.
Use the relation reaction Gibbs energy equals R T times the natural logarithm
of Q divided by K.
For an illustrative reaction at three hundred kelvin, let the dimensionless
equilibrium constant be ten and the current dimensionless reaction quotient
one
hundred.
The quotient exceeds the equilibrium constant.
Using R equal to eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin gives
reaction Gibbs energy plus five point seven four kilojoules per mole of
reaction.
The forward reaction is thermodynamically uphill at this composition, so the
reverse direction is favoured.
Yet the standard reaction Gibbs energy is minus R T logarithm ten, or minus
five point seven four kilojoules per mole.
There is no contradiction: the two values refer to different conditions.
At Q equal to K, actual reaction Gibbs energy is zero.
Activities are dimensionless; concentration ratios approximate them only under
suitable assumptions.
Thermodynamic preference does not specify how quickly equilibrium is
approached.
